passage.excerpt: We are a body knit together by a common religious profession, by unity of discipline, and by the bond of a common hope. We meet together as an assembly and a congregation. We pray together, we read scripture, we offer exhortation. Our presidents are elders, approved men. There is no buying and selling of any sort in the things of God. Even if there is a chest of sorts, it is not made up of purchase-money. On the monthly day, each puts in a small donation, if he will, and only if he be willing; for no one is compelled. These gifts are not spent on feasts or drinking bouts but to support and bury poor people, to supply the wants of boys and girls destitute of means and parents, and of old persons confined to the house.
passage.notes: Description of Christian assembly, common fund, and community life in Carthage

object_entity.proposition_label: God is three persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — in one substance
object_entity.description: The one God subsists in three persons (personae) — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — who share one substance (substantia); the Son proceeds from the Father and the Spirit from both, without dividing the divine substance.

evidence.notes: Tertullian Adv. Prax. 2 introduces Trinity vocabulary: una substantia, tres personae.

passage.excerpt: We do indeed believe that there is only one God, but under this dispensation, or oikonomia as we call it, the one God has also a Son, his Word, who proceeded from himself, by whom all things were made. Him we believe to have been sent by the Father into the virgin and to have been born of her — God and man, Son of God and Son of man. We believe him to have suffered, died, and been buried, to have risen again, to sit at the right hand of the Father, and to come to judge. He also sent from heaven the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, the sanctifier of the faith of those who believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
passage.notes: The rule of faith stated in trinitarian form; three persons, one God; oikonomia; foundational Latin trinitarian statement

source.title: Adversus Praxean
source.author: Tertullian
source.notes: Tertullian's anti-modalist treatise; ANF Vol. 3, Holmes translation.

evidence.notes: Tertullian Adv. Prax. 9 develops Father/Son distinction within one substance.

passage.excerpt: Bear always in mind that this is the rule of faith which I profess: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparable from each other. The Father is one, the Son another, the Spirit another — they are distinct, not separate. The Father is not the same as the Son, since they differ one from another in the mode of their being.
passage.notes: Distinct persons but inseparable; anti-modalist; trinitarian distinctions

evidence.notes: Tertullian De Praescr. 36 is addressed from and to the African/Carthaginian church.

passage.excerpt: Come now, you who wish to exercise your curiosity, run over the apostolic churches, in which the very seats of the apostles still preside at their own places; in which their authentic letters are read. Achaia is close to you — you have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia — you have Philippi, you have the Thessalonians. If you can go to Asia — you have Ephesus. But if you are near to Italy — you have Rome, whence our own authority derives also.
passage.notes: Apostolic sees as living witnesses to the faith; Rome, Corinth, Philippi, Ephesus named; authority of apostolic churches

source.author: Tertullian
source.notes: Tertullian's anti-modalist treatise; ANF Vol. 3, Holmes translation.

evidence.notes: Tertullian De Carne 5 reflects his Montanist-phase rigorist pneumatology.

passage.excerpt: The Son of God was crucified; I am not ashamed because men must needs be ashamed of it. And the Son of God died; it is by all means to be believed because it is absurd. And he was buried and rose again; the fact is certain because it is impossible. But how will all this be true in him, if he was not himself true — if he had not truly in himself that which might be crucified, might die, might be buried and might rise again? This is the flesh suffused with blood, built up with bones, interwoven with nerves, entwined with veins.
passage.notes: Certum est quia impossibile; defense of the reality of Christ's flesh and incarnation; anti-docetist
